abstract:
Do visual tasks have a relationship, or are they unrelated? For instance, could having surface normals simplify estimating the depth of an image? Intuition answers these questions positively, implying existence of a structure among visual tasks. Knowing this structure has notable values; it is the concept underlying transfer learning and provides a principled way for identifying redundancies across tasks, e.g., to seamlessly reuse supervision among related tasks or solve many tasks in one system without piling up the complexity.

We proposes a fully computational approach for modeling the structure of space of visual tasks. This is done via finding (first and higher-order) transfer learning dependencies across a dictionary of twenty six 2D, 2.5D, 3D, and semantic tasks in a latent space. The product is a computational taxonomic map for task transfer learning. We study the consequences of this structure, e.g. nontrivial emerged relationships, and exploit them to reduce the demand for labeled data. For example, we show that the total number of labeled datapoints needed for solving a set of 10 tasks can be reduced by roughly 23\\frac{2}{3} (compared to training independently) while keeping the performance nearly the same. We provide a set of tools for computing and probing this taxonomical structure including a solver that users can employ to devise efficient supervision policies for their use cases.

content.problem: Vision tasks are usually learned in isolation from scratch, which ignores their quantifiable relationships and leads to an enormous labeled data requirement.
content.proposed_solution: The authors propose a fully computational framework that measures first- and higher-order transfer dependencies among twenty-six visual tasks, normalizes transfer affinities with the Analytic Hierarchy Process, and uses Binary Integer Programming to extract a globally optimal transfer taxonomy under a limited supervision budget.
content.algorithm_or_model: Taskonomy (computational task taxonomy via transfer functions, AHP normalization, and BIP)
dataset_testbed: Taskonomy dataset (4 million annotated indoor scene images from about 600 buildings, created by the paper)

metrics.name: reduction in labeled datapoints needed
metrics.condition: solving a set of 10 tasks using the taxonomy transfer policy compared to training each task independently, with nearly the same performance

metrics.name: Spearman's rho
metrics.condition: correlation between taxonomy-predicted transfer ranking and Top-1 accuracy ranking for scene classification when fine-tuned on MIT Places

metrics.name: Spearman's rho
metrics.condition: correlation between taxonomy-predicted transfer ranking and Top-1 accuracy ranking for object classification when fine-tuned on ImageNet

metrics.name: win rate
metrics.condition: the paper's depth estimator versus the released models of Laina et al. on the test set

content.claim: A computationally discovered task taxonomy reduces the labeled data needed to solve a set of ten tasks by roughly two-thirds while keeping performance nearly the same, and the discovered structure remains stable, transfers to out-of-dictionary tasks, and correlates with transfer rankings on ImageNet and MIT Places.
author_stated_limitations: Although stability with respect to architectures and datasets was validated, the findings are in principle specific to the chosen models and data.
The modeling relies on a set of common human-defined visual tasks rather than computationally discovered latent subtasks in a compositional approach.
Generalization depends on the task dictionary being a proper sample of the dense task space, and more formal study is required for the outcome to be provably guaranteed in the general case.
The structure is computed in one go and lacks mechanisms for augmenting or expanding it as new tasks are mastered, which lifelong learning scenarios require.

evidence.problem_quote: Siloing tasks makes training a new task or a comprehensive perception system a Sisyphean challenge, whereby each task needs to be learned individually from scratch. Doing so ignores their quantifiably useful relationships leading to a massive labeled data requirement.
evidence.proposed_solution_quote: We proposes a fully computational approach for modeling the structure of space of visual tasks. This is done via finding (first and higher-order) transfer learning dependencies across a dictionary of twenty six 2D, 2.5D, 3D, and semantic tasks in a latent space.
evidence.claim_quote: For example, we show that the total number of labeled datapoints needed for solving a set of 10 tasks can be reduced by roughly 2/3 (compared to training independently) while keeping the performance nearly the same.
author_stated_limitation_quotes: Though we validated the stability of the findings w.r.t various architectures and datasets, it should be noted that the findings are in principle model and data specific.

We performed the modeling via a set of common human-defined visual tasks. It is natural to consider a further compositional approach in which such common tasks are viewed as *observed samples* which are composed of computationally found latent subtasks.

Though we showed a good tolerance w.r.t. to the choice of dictionary and transferring to out-of-dictionary tasks, this outcome holds upon a proper sampling of the space as a function of its regularity. More formal studies on properties of the computed space is required for this to be provably guaranteed for a general case.
We performed the modeling in one go. In many cases, e.g. lifelong learning, the system is evolving and the number of mastered tasks constantly increase.
